parent.name: Nimzowitsch Defense
parent.overview: Black develops a knight on move one and invites White to build a centre, planning to undermine it with timely pieces and pawn breaks (...d5, ...e5 or ...e6). The most common reply to 2.d4 is 2...d5 with 3.exd5 Qxd5 (Scandinavian-type), 3.e5 Bf5 (French-Advance-like with a freed bishop) or the 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.d5 Ne5 line, which is French-like in structure. Alternatively Black plays 2...e5 (Kennedy Variation), which can transpose to the Scotch, or 2...e6/2...g6 (Franco-Hiva, Pirc connection) with flexible set-ups. Kasparov and Keene wrote it has never been fully accepted as dependable, but sources agree it is far from refuted; players choose it to escape preparation and play non-standard but often French/Scandinavian-like middlegames. Roughly 2% of games per Chessable.

parent.name: Sicilian Defense
parent.overview: Black answers 1.e4 with ...c5 to trade a flank pawn for White's d-pawn, which leaves Black a central pawn majority and a half-open c-file in return for White's lead in development and space. This asymmetry is the point: Black plays for a win rather than equality. The usual pattern is White attacking on the kingside while Black counterattacks on the queenside along the c-file (...b5, ...Rc8), often with opposite-side castling in the sharpest lines. The root is a crossroads: after 2.Nf3 (about 80% of master games, s1) it branches into Najdorf, Dragon, Scheveningen, Classical, Sveshnikov, Taimanov and Kan, which range from forcing and theory-heavy (Najdorf, Dragon, Sveshnikov) to flexible and solid (Kan, Classical, Taimanov). White's anti-Sicilians (Alapin, Closed, Grand Prix, 2.d3) avoid the Open Sicilian and are quieter. The root as a whole is the most played and most analysed opening at club and master level (s1).

parent.name: Bird Opening: Dutch Variation
parent.overview: After 1.f4 d5 the game resembles a Dutch Defence with colours reversed and White a tempo up. White's main aims are control of e5 and the dark central squares with the f-pawn, usually 2.Nf3 followed either by a g3/Bg2 fianchetto or by e3, Be2, O-O and d3 or d4/c3 (Stonewall formation). Black meets it by fighting for the centre and the dark squares: a fianchetto with ...g6/...Bg7, or ...Nf6, ...e6 and ...c5, with ...Bg4 as a pin. The play is positional and both sides develop to optimal squares; the downside of f4 is a weakened kingside, so it is 'double-edged' for less experienced players. Sources say there is little theory, it can be a surprise weapon at club level, and the opening has been tried by strong players (Larsen, Carlsen, Nakamura, Karjakin) but is not popular at the top, with White scoring only about 46.7% overall.

parent.name: Sicilian Defense: Smith-Morra Gambit
parent.overview: White offers a pawn on move 2 (2.d4 cxd4 3.c3) to swap the d-pawn for Black's c-pawn, gain a lead in development and open the c- and d-files. After 3...dxc3 4.Nxc3 White plays Nf3, Bc4 and quick castling, aiming at f7 with the Bc4, a Qe2/Rd1/Rc1 battery and tactical shots such as Nd5 and e5. Black either accepts and consolidates (typically with ...Nc6, ...e6, ...a6, ...Nge7-g6 or a Scheveningen/Kan set-up, trading pieces to hold the pawn) or declines with 3...Nf6, reaching a safe Alapin Sicilian. Play is open and tactical with White chasing the initiative; if Black consolidates the extra pawn he has good endgame chances.

parent.name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit
parent.overview: White offers a pawn with 1.d4 d5 2.e4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3, aiming for rapid development, the open f-file and a kingside attack with Bc4, Nge2 or Bf4, castling, g4/h4 and Qe1-h4 ideas against h7. Black accepts with 4...exf3 5.Nxf3 and can choose among the Euwe (5...e6), Ziegler (5...c6), Teichmann (5...Bg4) and Bogoljubov (5...g6) defences, or decline with the Lemberger Countergambit 3...e5. With accurate defence Black consolidates the pawn, trades pieces and heads for a better endgame; engines and master opinion call White's compensation insufficient, which is why it is almost never seen at top level. Below master level it scores very well because the attack is easy to play and hard to defend against. The game is typically open and tactical.

parent.name: English Defense
parent.overview: Black plays 1...b6 (or 1...e6 2.c4 b6) intending ...Bb7, a hypermodern set-up in which the bishop on b7 pressures e4 and the centre rather than occupying it. After 3.e4 Bb7 White builds a broad pawn centre (Bd3, f3, Nc3) and Black undermines it with ...Bb4(+), ...f5 and sometimes ...Qh4, as in Polugaevsky-Korchnoi 1977 (4.Qc2 Qh4 5.Nd2 Bb4). The play is double-edged: Black gives White space and a strong centre, then goes for counterplay and tactics against it. Gambit versions (Hartlaub 4...f5, Polli 4.f3 f5) and 3.Nc3 Bb4 transpositions to a ...b6 Nimzo-Indian are the main branches. It was a surprise weapon of Speelman, Short, Miles and Keene in the 1980s and is rare in elite play, although some club players use 1...b6/2...Bb7 as a universal system.

parent.name: Petrov's Defense
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nf6 3. Nxe5 d6
parent.overview: Black answers 2.Nf3 by counter-attacking e4 rather than defending e5. After 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.d4 d5 6.Bd3 both sides have lost an e-pawn and the structure is symmetrical, with the e-file the main open line. Black's aim is to equalise by quick development and piece trades; White tries to turn a small lead in development or slightly freer play into pressure, often castling and using the e-file or a queenside castling and pawn storm. The 3.d4 Steinitz line (3...Nxe4 4.Bd3 d5 5.Nxe5 Nd7) and 3.Nc3 (Four Knights transposition) or 3.d3 sidelines give quieter or more varied structures. The main lines are widely played at the top and are known as drawish, though some lines hold real attacking chances for both sides.

parent.name: Englund Gambit
parent.overview: Black answers 1.d4 with 1...e5, offering the e-pawn after 2.dxe5 to avoid closed queen's-pawn positions and set tactical problems. The main line is 2...Nc6 3.Nf3 Qe7 4.Bf4 Qb4+ 5.Bd2 Qxb2 6.Nc3, where Black regains the pawn on b2 but loses the queenside attack; the gambit relies on traps such as 6.Bc3?? Bb4! with mate threats on c1. White can simply keep the pawn and, with accurate development, retains an advantage. Strong players and engines consider it unsound for Black, and top-level players almost never choose it. It scores through quick development and traps against an unprepared opponent.

parent.name: Polish Opening
parent.overview: White plays 1.b4 to grab queenside space and fianchetto the bishop to b2, putting long-diagonal pressure on e5, f6 and g7. It is an irregular flank opening: Black chooses the set-up with 1...e5 (2.Bb2 Bxb4 3.Bxe5, the Exchange Variation, which equalises), 1...d5 (the German Defence 2...Qd6 etc.), or 1...Nf6 and 1...e6 reaching Indian-like or Queen's Gambit-like set-ups. The opening is sound and not refuted but gives Black no real problems, so it is rarely seen at elite level and chosen as a surprise weapon (Carlsen used it against Nakamura and So in 2021). Theory is small and the play is flank-oriented, with unbalanced pawn structures but typically no early forced tactics. Alekhine's complaint was that it reveals White's intentions before knowing Black's.

parent.name: Slav Defense
parent.overview: Black supports d5 with ...c6 so that the centre is held by pawns while the light-squared bishop stays free to come out (usually to f5 or g4) before ...e6. The root is a crossroads: after 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3 Black chooses the Pure Slav with ...dxc4 (active bishop, ...e5/...c5 breaks), the Semi-Slav with ...e6 (c6-d5-e6 triangle, theory-heavy and often sharp: Meran, Botvinnik, Anti-Meran), or the Chebanenko ...a6. White can also play the Exchange (cxd5 cxd5), a symmetrical structure with queenside minority attack ideas that has a drawish reputation, or quiet systems with 3.e3 or 3.Bf4. The Slav is played by many world champions (Botvinnik, Smyslov, Anand, Kramnik) and is regarded as sound; sources treat it as solid with room for counterplay rather than a forced-draw defence.

parent.name: Dutch Defense
parent.overview: Black answers 1.d4 with 1...f5, fighting for e4 and avoiding symmetrical play, at the cost of weakening the kingside (the e8-h5 diagonal) and the e6 square. Three set-ups dominate: the Leningrad (...g6, ...Bg7, KID-style, with ...e5 or ...Ne4 and kingside play), the Stonewall (...e6, ...d5, ...c6 with a knight on e4 and a bad light-squared bishop) and the Classical (...e6, ...Be7, ...d6, later ...e5). White usually fianchettoes with g3/Bg2 and c4 and prepares e4 or queenside expansion, or sidesteps theory with the Staunton Gambit (2.e4), Hopton or Korchnoi Attack (h3 and g4). Sources agree it is sound but double-edged, unbalancing and theoretical, played occasionally by Carlsen, Nakamura and Nepomniachtchi but never a main defence to 1.d4.
